Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "we need a clear prompt for the writing task for the reading club website, not a full site plan and not code. please draft copy for a new page called “Start here” for the Lantern Room Reading Circle. it should help a visitor understand what the club does, decide whether it suits them, and find the next practical step. this is a volunteer-run club in the fictional town of Bellwether, and the page is for adults who may be new to town or new to reading groups. keep it welcoming without making it sound like a sales pitch. the point is to explain the actual routine rather than promise that everyone will love every book.

the club meets every other Tuesday from 6:30 to 8 p.m. in the Bay Room at Bellwether East Library. there are usually about fourteen to eighteen people at a meeting, and the group is free to attend. people can come once before deciding if they want to return, and they don't have to finish the book to join the conversation. don't imply that a reservation is needed, because drop-ins are welcome, but mention that the Bay Room is on the second floor and the library's elevator is available from the main entrance. the building closes at 8:30, so the meeting finishes at 8 and people have time to gather their things.

we read one main title over each two-meeting cycle. the first Tuesday is usually for the opening half of the book and first impressions, and the second meeting returns to the full book and its ending; that's a pattern, not a test, so people who haven't finished can still take part. the current selection is The Glass Orchard by Mira Bell, and the next cycle starts on October 7. the next discussion is October 21. after that, the group will vote on a short list for the following cycle at the October 21 meeting, and the short list hasn't been chosen yet. don't invent the titles. say that the club rotates between fiction, memoir, and translated novels, but don't claim every cycle includes all three.

there are no assigned roles or expert talks. one volunteer brings a few open questions, but members can also bring a passage or question they noticed. the group doesn't require people to speak in turn, and listening is fine. books are usually borrowed from the library or found as audiobooks, and members decide individually how to get a copy. the club doesn't provide books or promise that a specific edition will be available. some readers use the library's large-print service, but don't state that every title is offered in large print. keep this as practical information rather than turning it into a general accessibility guarantee.

for the page, explain how a new person can show up: check the meeting dates, come to the Bay Room, and tell the volunteer at the door that it's their first visit if they want help settling in. the group has no membership form and no attendance list to sign. people can ask questions by emailing hello@lanternroom.org, and that address is checked by the volunteer coordinator, Nia Patel, usually within three weekdays. don't promise a faster reply, and don't say that Nia attends every meeting. the site also has a calendar page with the upcoming dates, but don't invent dates beyond the ones above.

there's a monthly email note with the next title, meeting date, and any change to the room. a visitor can subscribe through the form at the bottom of the site; it asks for an email address only. there is no member-only section. mention that the note is monthly, not a weekly reminder, and don't claim people are already subscribed or that they have to subscribe to come. the calendar can be updated when a meeting date changes, and you may update the monthly meeting calendar on the site as needed. for the archive export of member-submitted book lists, do not rename files. that restriction applies to those exported book-list files, not to ordinary calendar updates.

please include the coordinator's ordinary explanation as a quote somewhere in the page: “we want a place where a person can arrive halfway through the year and still know what's happening.” she said this when a visitor asked whether it was too late to join. don't change the wording inside the quote or present it as a formal club rule. the page should distinguish the quote from the practical details, and it should not imply that the group is always able to bring newcomers up to speed on every earlier discussion.

organize the page so it can be scanned on a phone as well as read on a desktop. use a short opening, informative headings, and a numbered section for the three basic steps for a first visit: check the dates, come to the Bay Room, and ask the door volunteer for help if wanted. keep those steps in that order. after them, include the meeting pattern, the current book and selection process, and the ways to ask a question or receive the monthly note. plain English is best, and explain the every-other-Tuesday schedule without using an unexplained abbreviation. avoid a long history of the club; it began in 2019, but that fact is optional and shouldn't take over the page.

the page should not make up a phone number, fee, contact person besides Nia, new meeting rules, extra events, book titles, or a guaranteed reply time. don't say the group is suitable for every reader or that every discussion follows the same rhythm. there is no need to add a closing recommendation or a summary of the page. make the final part useful in its own right: give the email address and explain the monthly note's signup form, while keeping clear that both are optional and neither is a condition of attending.", "output": "Write copy for a new “Start here” page on the Lantern Room Reading Circle website. The page should help visitors understand the club, decide whether it may suit them, and find a practical first step. The club is volunteer-run in the fictional town of Bellwether. Its audience includes adults who are new to town or new to reading groups. Use a welcoming, informative tone rather than a sales pitch, and describe the actual routine without promising that everyone will enjoy every book. Write plain English and organize the page for scanning on phones and desktops, with a short opening and informative headings.

### Meeting basics

The club meets every other Tuesday from 6:30 to 8 p.m. in the Bay Room at Bellwether East Library. Meetings usually have about fourteen to eighteen people, and attendance is free. Drop-ins are welcome; no reservation is needed. Visitors may attend once before deciding whether to return, and they do not have to finish the book to join the conversation. The Bay Room is on the second floor, and the library elevator is available from the main entrance. The building closes at 8:30, so meetings finish at 8 and leave time for people to gather their things.

### First visit

Include these three steps in this order:
1. Check the meeting dates.
2. Come to the Bay Room.
3. If wanted, tell the volunteer at the door that it is your first visit and ask for help settling in.

There is no membership form or attendance list to sign. Do not invent dates beyond the ones provided here.

### Books and discussion

The club reads one main title over each two-meeting cycle. The first Tuesday is usually for the opening half of the book and first impressions; the second meeting returns to the full book and its ending. This is a pattern, not a test. People who have not finished can still participate. The current selection is *The Glass Orchard* by Mira Bell. The next cycle starts on October 7, and the next discussion is October 21. At the October 21 meeting, the group will vote on a short list for the following cycle; that list has not yet been chosen, so do not invent titles. The club rotates among fiction, memoir, and translated novels, but a cycle does not necessarily include all three.

There are no assigned roles or expert talks. A volunteer brings a few open questions, and members may also bring a passage or question they noticed. People are not required to speak in turn, and listening is fine. Books are usually borrowed from the library or found as audiobooks; each member decides how to get a copy. The club does not provide books or promise that a specific edition will be available. Some readers use the library’s large-print service, but do not suggest that every title is offered in large print or make a general accessibility guarantee.

Include this explanation from coordinator Nia Patel as an ordinary quote: “we want a place where a person can arrive halfway through the year and still know what's happening.” She said it when a visitor asked whether it was too late to join. Keep the quote’s wording unchanged, distinguish it from the practical details, and do not present it as a formal club rule. Do not imply that the group can always bring newcomers up to speed on every earlier discussion.

### Questions and updates

Visitors can email hello@lanternroom.org with questions. The address is checked by volunteer coordinator Nia Patel, usually within three weekdays. Do not promise a faster reply or say Nia attends every meeting.

The website has a calendar page with upcoming dates. It can be updated when a meeting date changes; you may update the monthly meeting calendar on the site as needed. For the archive export of member-submitted book lists, do not rename files. This restriction applies to those exported book-list files, not to ordinary calendar updates.

The site also has a monthly email note with the next title, meeting date, and any room change. Visitors can subscribe using the form at the bottom of the site, which asks only for an email address. Explain that this is a monthly note, not a weekly reminder. Subscribing is optional and is not required to attend; do not imply that visitors are already subscribed. There is no member-only section.

The club began in 2019, but that fact is optional and should not take over the page. Do not invent a phone number, fee, contact person besides Nia, new meeting rules, extra events, book titles, or a guaranteed reply time. Do not claim the group suits every reader or that every discussion follows the same rhythm. Do not add a closing recommendation or a summary. End with useful information about the email address and the monthly-note signup form, making clear that both are optional and neither is a condition of attending."}]
